title: Building a Production Design System That Scaled Across Products
background: As the Tignis product suite expanded, multiple teams began shipping interfaces independently, which led to inconsistent UI patterns, duplicated component logic, and slower development cycles. What started as small variations across features gradually became a systemic issue, making the product harder to maintain and more difficult for users to navigate with confidence.
role:
To address this, I led the design and implementation of a unified design system that standardized both the visual language and the underlying front-end architecture. The goal was not just consistency, but to create a system that reduced friction between design and engineering and allowed teams to ship faster with fewer repeated decisions.

I owned the system end-to-end, from early audit and system definition through to production implementation in React. This included defining the design language in Figma, structuring reusable components, and working directly in code to ensure the system held up under real product constraints.

Rather than treating this as a design-only initiative, I approached it as a shared system between design and engineering. My focus was on ensuring that what we designed could be implemented cleanly, reused reliably, and scaled across multiple teams without introducing additional complexity.
design:
Research & Audit

I began by conducting a comprehensive UI audit across existing applications to identify inconsistencies in typography, color usage, spacing, and component behaviors. I also interviewed developers to understand common friction points when implementing UI.

Ideation & System Architecture

Using these insights, I structured the design system around a set of core primitives that could map directly to code. Design tokens were defined for color, typography, and spacing, and were aligned with a centralized theming approach. Component structures in Figma were intentionally designed to mirror how they would be implemented in React, reducing translation gaps between design and development.

Prototyping & Documentation

Instead of relying solely on static mocks, I created high-fidelity prototypes that reflected real interaction behavior and edge cases. This made it possible to validate complex flows earlier and ensured that components were designed with realistic data and usage patterns in mind.

Implementation

I partnered closely with engineering to implement the system using React, with Material UI serving as a foundational layer. Rather than using it out of the box, I extended and customized its theming and component structure to align with our product’s specific needs and interaction patterns. A key focus during implementation was maintaining parity between the design system and the codebase. Component APIs were designed to reflect the same structure and variants defined in Figma, which reduced ambiguity and made it easier for engineers to adopt the system without additional interpretation.This alignment between design and code allowed the system to function as a true shared language, rather than two parallel systems that required constant translation.
challenges:
One of the primary challenges was balancing flexibility with consistency. Product teams needed the ability to create unique experiences, while engineering needed predictable patterns to maintain performance and scalability.

To address this, I created component variants and clear usage guidelines, allowing teams to achieve visual diversity without breaking the system. I also ensured the React components mirrored the Figma library structure, reducing translation issues between design and code.
impact:
The design system became the foundation for how multiple teams built and shipped interfaces across the product suite. By shifting from one-off component creation to a shared system, we reduced redundant work and improved the overall speed and quality of development.

Key outcomes included:

  • Faster feature development through reusable components
  • Improved UI consistency across the product suite
  • Reduced design and engineering rework
  • Streamlined onboarding for new developers and designers

More importantly, this work shifted how teams approached UI development. Instead of treating each feature as a standalone effort, teams were able to build on top of a shared foundation, allowing the product to scale more predictably as complexity increased.

title: Implementing a User-Centered Design Process
background: Early product features were often built based on internal assumptions rather than validated user needs. This sometimes resulted in features requiring multiple revisions after release. To improve alignment with customer workflows and reduce costly rework, we adopted a more structured user-centered design process.
role: I introduced and led an iterative design workflow that emphasized early concept validation through prototypes and structured user feedback. I collaborated with product managers, engineers, and customers to ensure design decisions were informed by real-world usage.
design:
Research

I worked with product and customer success teams to gather qualitative insights from existing users. This included identifying common pain points, observing how users navigated the platform, and understanding their goals within the product.

Ideation

Based on these insights, I developed low-fidelity wireframes to explore multiple potential solutions. These early concepts allowed us to quickly iterate without committing to detailed visual design.

Prototyping

Once promising directions were identified, I created high-fidelity interactive prototypes in Figma. These prototypes simulated real workflows, allowing stakeholders and clients to experience the proposed features before development began.

Testing & Feedback

We conducted feedback sessions with internal stakeholders and select customers. Observing how users interacted with the prototypes helped identify usability issues early and refine the design before handoff to engineering.
challenges:
A key challenge was shifting internal expectations. Some stakeholders initially preferred jumping straight to development rather than investing time in early validation.

To address this, I demonstrated how prototype testing could quickly uncover usability issues that would be far more expensive to fix after implementation. As teams began seeing the value of early validation, this iterative approach became a standard part of the workflow.
impact:
The new design process had several measurable benefits:

  • Reduced feature rework during development
  • Faster alignment between product, design, and engineering
  • Increased confidence in product decisions before development investment
  • Stronger alignment between product features and real user workflows

By integrating research, prototyping, and validation into the development lifecycle, we were able to design solutions that more effectively addressed real customer needs.

title: Interactive Prototypes and Event Demonstrations
background: Tignis frequently engaged with potential clients at industry events such as SemiCon. However, demonstrating complex product capabilities in live environments posed challenges, particularly when reliable internet access was not guaranteed. To support sales and marketing efforts, we needed interactive prototypes that could effectively showcase the platform’s value in a controlled and reliable way.
role: I designed and developed interactive demo prototypes used in client presentations and industry events. These demos simulated key product workflows and allowed stakeholders to explore features in a guided, hands-on way.
design:
Research & Planning

I collaborated with sales, product, and leadership teams to identify the most compelling product features for prospective customers. We focused on scenarios that clearly demonstrated the platform’s value and differentiated it from competitors.

Ideation

I mapped out demo flows that highlighted key capabilities while keeping the experience intuitive and engaging. These flows were designed to simulate realistic user scenarios rather than static feature showcases.

Prototyping

Using design tools and front-end development technologies, I created interactive prototypes that closely resembled the actual product experience. These included realistic data visualizations, navigation patterns, and workflows.

Validation

Before events, I tested the prototypes internally with sales and product teams to ensure they aligned with messaging and could be easily presented during client conversations.
challenges:
The primary challenge was balancing technical realism with reliability. A full product demo could be unstable or dependent on live data, while a static mockup lacked interactivity.

The solution was to create interactive demo environments that simulated real product behavior while remaining fully controlled and stable, including offline functionality when necessary.
impact:
These prototypes became valuable tools for both sales and product strategy.

  • More engaging product demonstrations at industry events
  • Increased confidence during client presentations
  • Stronger alignment between product capabilities and sales messaging
  • Faster validation of potential product features before committing to development

The demos also helped leadership visualize future product directions, influencing roadmap discussions and strategic decisions.

title: Telehealth Appointment Management App
background:
As healthcare continues to evolve, the demand for telehealth services has surged, particularly due to the global pandemic. Recognizing the need for a seamless, integrated system, I set out to design and develop a mobile app that would streamline appointment scheduling and patient-doctor communication for a medical clinic.

patient-doctor communication for a medical clinic. The app was designed to serve both medical professionals (doctors, receptionists) and patients by providing a user-friendly platform for appointment booking, real-time communication with doctors, and essential medical consultations. The goal was to create a system that reduced the administrative burden on receptionists, minimized appointment scheduling conflicts, and provided a more accessible way for patients to connect with their healthcare providers without leaving their homes.
role:
I took on a multifaceted role throughout this project, overseeing all aspects from research and design to development:

  • Research & User Interviews: Conducted interviews with doctors, medical receptionists, and patients to understand their pain points and needs.
  • Design: Led the design of the user interface, focusing on accessibility and simplicity for medical professionals and patients.
  • Prototyping: Developed interactive prototypes for user testing and iterative feedback.
  • Development: Built the app using React. Next.js, and TypeScript, integrating scheduling features, telehealth functionality, and user authentication.
  • Testing & Launch: Coordinated user testing cycles with real users (doctors and patients), then refined the product based on feedback before launching.
design:
Ideation & Research

To better understand the target users, I conducted in-depth interviews with three key groups:

  • Doctors: Focused on their need for an easy-to-use system for managing patient appointments and providing quick consultations. They requested features like secure video consultations, easy patient record access, and notifications for appointment changes.
  • Receptionists: I discovered that they were often burdened by manual scheduling and dealing with last-minute cancellations. The ability to quickly see doctor availability and reschedule appointments efficiently was a priority.
  • Patients: I gathered feedback on their expectations for telehealth services. Key pain points included complicated booking systems and the difficulty of getting quick access to doctors. Features like a simple appointment scheduling process, real-time communication with doctors, and the ability to view medical records were critical.

I also analyzed the existing solutions in the market (such as MyChart and Teladoc) to understand both the strengths and gaps in these platforms.

User Flows and Wireframing

Based on insights from the interviews, I developed several user flows and wireframes that outlined how patients would schedule appointments, interact with their doctors, and manage their health information. Additionally, I mapped out workflows for medical staff, ensuring they could efficiently manage appointments, view patient information, and initiate consultations.

Key screens designed included:

  • Patient Dashboard: Displays upcoming appointments, recent messages, and quick links to schedule or reschedule appointments.
  • Doctor Dashboard: Provides a list of scheduled appointments, with patient details, options to start video consultations, and the ability to send follow-up messages.
  • Appointment Booking System: Allows patients to view available time slots for their doctor, book appointments, and receive reminders.

UI Design

Once the wireframes were approved, I created high-fidelity designs. Given the medical context, I focused on:

  • Simplicity and Clarity: The design had to be intuitive for users of varying ages and technical skills. I used large buttons, clear typography, and easy-to-follow navigation.
  • Color Palette: I opted for a calming, healthcare-inspired palette with soft blues and greens, creating a reassuring and professional aesthetic.
  • Accessibility: I incorporated accessibility features such as high-contrast modes and text resizing to ensure the app was usable by patients with visual impairments.
challenges:
Challenge 1: Secure Video Consultations

A critical requirement was ensuring secure, HIPAA-compliant video consultations within the app. This was a challenge because security is paramount in the healthcare industry.

Solution: I integrated a secure video consultation API that provided end-to-end encryption. The video call feature was designed to be easily accessible via the doctor’s dashboard, allowing them to initiate calls with a single click.

Challenge 2: Appointment Scheduling Conflicts

Managing appointment overlaps and last-minute changes posed a challenge, especially with doctors’ schedules often changing due to emergencies or patient cancellations.

Solution: I developed a dynamic scheduling system that allowed real-time updates. The system automatically notified patients and receptionists of changes and provided alternate available slots to prevent overbooking.

Challenge 3: User Onboarding

Given that many patients, especially elderly individuals, were not familiar with telehealth apps, a streamlined onboarding process was essential.

Solution: I implemented a step-by-step onboarding flow that guided users through creating an account, booking their first appointment, and using the video consultation features. Additionally, I provided clear instructions and tooltips throughout the app.
impact:
User Engagement

After launching the app, the clinic experienced a 40% reduction in phone calls to the reception desk, as patients were able to schedule appointments directly through the app. Doctors reported less time spent on administrative tasks, allowing them to focus more on patient care.

Patient Satisfaction

Patients reported a high level of satisfaction, with 85% saying the app made scheduling easier and 90% appreciating the ability to have consultations without visiting the clinic. The feedback emphasized the importance of the real-time communication feature, which allowed patients to ask questions and receive timely responses.

Business Impact

The clinic saw a 25% increase in telehealth consultations within the first three months post-launch, as the app improved accessibility and convenience for patients. Additionally, the administrative team experienced a 30% reduction in appointment scheduling errors, improving overall clinic efficiency.

title: Designing a Lead-Collection App Using RFID for Conference and Convention Networking
background:
Networking is a cornerstone of conferences and conventions, and with the rise of digital tools, many exhibitors and event organizers seek more efficient ways to collect and manage leads. I was tasked with designing a mobile app that would streamline the process of lead collection by utilizing RFID (Radio Frequency Identification) technology. The app allowed exhibitors to scan badges worn by conference attendees, capturing valuable information such as name, company, email, and areas of interest, all in real-time.

The app was built to support a variety of events, but the primary focus for testing and deployment was at Exhibitors Live in Las Vegas, where I was sent to gather firsthand feedback and observe how attendees and exhibitors interacted with the app. The goal was to enhance the app’s functionality, user experience, and design to ensure it met the needs of users in real-world settings.
role:
As the sole UX/UI designer for this project, I was responsible for:

  • Research & User Feedback: Conducting surveys and interviews with both exhibitors and attendees during the conference.
  • UX Design: Designing the app’s user flow, ensuring it was intuitive for users with varying levels of tech experience.
  • UI Design: Creating the visual interface, focusing on accessibility and efficiency.
  • Prototyping & Iteration: Building interactive prototypes and refining the design based on user testing feedback.
  • On-Site Testing: Attending Exhibitors Live to observe how users interacted with the app in real-time and gather valuable feedback through surveys and interviews.
design:
Ideation & Research

The first step in the design process involved understanding the user needs of both exhibitors and attendees. To do this, I interviewed potential users, including exhibitors who needed to capture leads and attendees who were often approached by multiple companies.

I conducted secondary research into existing lead-collection systems, particularly those used in trade shows and conferences. Many of the systems were either too complex or not integrated with other event management tools, leading to frustrations during the lead capture and follow-up process.

For this app, the main user needs were:

  • Exhibitors: A quick and easy way to scan badges, access captured lead information in real-time, and categorize leads by interest or priority.
  • Attendees: A seamless experience when interacting with exhibitors, knowing their information would be instantly shared without any manual input.

User Flows and Wireframing

I created user flows for both exhibitors and attendees:

  • Exhibitor Flow: From opening the app, scanning a badge, and categorizing the lead to generating a report or exporting the data.
  • Attendee Flow: Ensuring that scanning a badge was smooth and unobtrusive, with a confirmation screen showing the attendee’s info after scanning.

With these flows in mind, I created wireframes to determine the layout of key screens, including:

  • The Lead Capture Screen: Where the exhibitor could scan a badge and see the attendee’s information immediately.
  • The Lead Management Screen: Where exhibitors could organize, tag, and categorize leads for easy follow-up.
  • A Dashboard: Showing key metrics such as total leads captured, lead types, and scanning history.

UI Design

Once the wireframes were approved, I moved to high-fidelity designs. I focused on:

  • Clean, Minimalistic UI: The design had to be efficient, with minimal clutter so exhibitors could scan badges and access information quickly.
  • Color Palette: I used a professional, tech-forward palette with blues and whites to convey trust and clarity, keeping it neutral so the focus remained on the information being captured.
  • Accessibility: I ensured the interface was easy to navigate, with larger touch targets and simple, intuitive icons.

The design also needed to be flexible for various screen sizes, since the app would be used on both phones and tablets, often in fast-paced, high-traffic environments like conventions.

User Research & Feedback

Before and during the conference, I conducted surveys and interviews with users (both exhibitors and attendees) to gather insights:

  • Exhibitors: Many exhibitors struggled with slow or inefficient lead capture methods, often relying on pen-and-paper or manual data entry, which led to errors. They needed a system that could help them categorize leads on the fly and quickly follow up.
  • Attendees: Attendees wanted a simple process where their information was shared automatically, without having to manually input anything or engage with cumbersome forms.
challenges:
Challenge 1: Badge Scanning Accuracy

RFID technology can sometimes be finicky in crowded, high-traffic environments like conventions, leading to occasional failed scans.

Solution: I implemented a retry mechanism in the app that would automatically attempt to scan the badge again if the first attempt failed. Additionally, a manual entry option was provided for when scanning failed repeatedly.

Challenge 2: Data Privacy and Transparency

Attendees were concerned about what data was being shared with exhibitors when their badges were scanned.

Solution: I added a clear confirmation screen after a badge was scanned that displayed the attendee's information and explicitly stated what data would be shared with the exhibitor. This helped improve trust in the app.

Challenge 3: Lead Categorization on the Fly

Exhibitors wanted an efficient way to categorize leads quickly without interrupting the scanning process.

Solution: I added a simple tagging system that allowed exhibitors to categorize leads with a single tap after scanning a badge. This streamlined the process and reduced the risk of lost or misclassified leads.
impact:
User Engagement

After launching the app at Exhibitors Live, exhibitor feedback was overwhelmingly positive. 90% of exhibitors reported that the app made lead collection more efficient and streamlined. Many stated that it helped them engage with more attendees than they would have through traditional methods, such as paper forms or QR codes.

Lead Collection Efficiency

Exhibitors captured 30% more leads compared to previous events where they used manual data entry or QR code systems. The app’s speed and ease of use were critical in increasing the volume of leads collected.

Business Impact

The app helped exhibitors reduce the time spent on administrative tasks (like entering lead information into a database), allowing them to spend more time on quality interactions with attendees. Additionally, the app provided exhibitors with easy access to lead data post-event, facilitating faster follow-up and increasing conversion rates.
